#828. ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance

Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City

Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so.

Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser.

Another City attack comes down their right: after Jair Cunha’s clearing header from a deep Matheus Nunes cross, the ball loops up in the air before descending inside the home penalty area.

Ryan Yates, Forest’s old-fashioned midfield general, is being pressed from behind by the Argentina international Enzo Fernández as the ball drops. Yates stands his ground, using his strength to hold off his opponent’s muscular challenge. Fernández tries to impose himself, too, but ends up on the turf.

Not only does Yates win that crucial one-on-one, by cleverly improvising an overhead kick to shift the ball away from danger he inadvertently begins a counterattack that arguably changes the course of Forest’s season.

Liam Delap shepherds the ball to Morgan Gibbs-White. Enzo Maresca’s team are hopelessly exposed and Gibbs-White devours the space in front of him with a driving run.

He lays a pass off to Delap, who takes one touch before swerving a sensational shot into the far corner for 3-1. It is a memorable move that will surely compete for goal of the month. But none of it would have been possible without the dirty work of Yates: a show of strength and desire from the captain at the other end of the pitch.

Oliver Glasner understands the importance of the moment and sprints to celebrate with his players. After a barren scoring run Delap suddenly has two goals in one afternoon. The home fans are delirious. Twelve seconds after Yates won the duel, Forest have a two-goal cushion rather than a desperate fight to maintain their lead.

The second ball is a pleasingly old-school term but remains of paramount importance. Visit your local amateur club and you are likely to hear it being shouted as a motivational mantra.

At grassroots level it’s a reminder to teammates that finesse and creativity are all very well, but it’s hard work, desire and a refusal to let your opponent get the better of you that win matches.

And it remains part of the elite game’s lexicon. Premier League managers sometimes point to upcoming opponents’ second-ball prowess – a back-handed compliment if ever there was one. The hidden meaning: “They feed off scraps at set pieces. They don’t create from open play.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

After seeing Southampton Under-21s lose to Wealdstone in the National League Cup a couple of years ago, I mentioned to the then Saints manager, Simon Rusk, that his goalkeeper had been shouting “second ball” throughout.

“To be honest,” Rusk replied with amusing frankness, “I’m not sure some of them even know what second ball means.”

Managers like relying on data. They like predictable outcomes. They prefer to remove risk, reduce chaos and exert control over as much of the game as possible. But while the outcome of a one-on-one duel can never be certain, the consequences can often be far-reaching. That’s why second balls matter.

Against City Yates was named in Forest’s starting lineup, and given the captain’s armband, for the first time this season. Glasner, asked how he had motivated his players, revealed: “Ryan Yates spoke. I played more than 500 games as a player, I’ve managed, I don’t know, 500 games … and I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech.”

Glasner’s captain backed up stirring words with action. If there was a sense Yates’s star was fading – that his attributes of graft, tenacity and box-to-box drive were losing currency – then it was emphatically extinguished at the City Ground.

Win the first one if you can. But it’s the second ball that often makes the difference.

#826. 'Unfinished business' - Tuchel committed to England

Thomas Tuchel has been England head coach since January 2025

England head coach Thomas Tuchel says he has "no intention" of leaving the job before Euro 2028 regardless of any offers from major clubs.

Tuchel succeeded Gareth Southgate as England boss in 2025 and signed an extension in February until Euro 2028, which will be co-hosted by England.

Manchester United are in advanced talks with USA men's coach Mauricio Pochettino over replacing Michael Carrick as head coach.

The Red Devils will need to activate a release clause in Pochettino's contract to hire the Argentine, believed to be in the region of around Â£7m.

But Tuchel says his contract does not include a release clause and he does not intend to leave his role to return to club management.

"I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros," he said. "I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business."

England lost the past two Euros finals under Southgate before Tuchel led the Three Lions to the semi-finals of his first major tournament, this summer's World Cup.

However, the former Bayern Munich, Chelsea and Paris St-Germain boss did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his England contract.

"I miss the 50 matches [a season]," he said.

"I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it's like the best two minutes, everything is done and you're in a full stadium, lights are on and you're just so excited and you're part of it."

England are second in their Nations League group and have two more group games over the coming days.

Tuchel's side host Croatia on Thursday before facing World Cup winners and group leaders Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

#825. General Hospital’s Randall England Dead at 75

Randall England—who played General Hospital villain Jack Slater in the 1980s—died on Sept. 25 following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to his family. He was 75.

Port Charles is feeling a little bit emptier.

Randall England—who was best known for his role as General Hospital villain Jack Slater during the 1980s—died on Sept. 25 in Los Angeles following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to his family. He was 75.

"Randall had the good fortune of surrounding himself with a wonderfully varied and interesting circle of people," read his online obituary. "Charming, loving, and generous with his time and energy, Randall was someone people could count on."

The tribute continued, "His legacy lives on in the people he loved, taught, and supported."

Born in 1951 in Oklahoma City, Okla., England began his career as a model before studying acting in New York. According to his obituary, a brief trip to Los Angeles for an audition "became a home," with the actor settling down in Beverly Hills.

He was first introduced on General Hospital in 1984, playing a stranger who arrives in Port Charles posing as a film producer. He remained on the soap opera for nearly year before his character was killed off in a dramatic shootout.

In addition to General Hospital, England appeared on iconic TV shows such as Dallas, The Young and the Restless and Baywatch. His other acting credits include 2003's Hellborn, 2008's Beverly Hills Chihuahua and Maroon 5’s 2015 music video for “Sugar.

But, according to England's family, his favorite role was being a dad to daughter Micaela Reed—who he shared with Jennifer Leigh Herreras—as well as "Pappaw" to grandkids Katherine Reed and Julian Reed.

"Friends, family, and former students have remembered his authenticity and the steady presence he offered in their lives," they wrote in his obituary. "He offered encouragement and advice freely."

"He was well known for his fashion sense, with stylish cowboy boots a fixture of his signature uniform for many years," England's family added. "Beverly Hills won’t be the same without him cruising around in his vintage BMW, sporting his dark Ray-Ban sunglasses."

#824. NASA unveils $10 billion in moon base contracts, new lunar missions and the 'PROMISE' of a nuclear-powered rover

The new contracts aim to pave the way for a permanent moon base.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA is pushing ahead with its plan to build a moon base for astronauts by 2032, with the agency unveiling up to $10 billion in contracts to launch and deliver cargo to the moon and other efforts on Saturday (Nov. 7).

The NASA announcement, revealed here during the space agency's "Max Power" air show event at Kennedy Space Center, included plans for a new $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) framework, dubbed CLPS 2, about$1.3 billion in funding for the agency's Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program, and the nuclear-powered "PROMISE" rover on the moon.

The announcements mark another step in NASA's effort to establish infrastructure on the moon before Artemis astronauts return to its surface, including a rover and other cargo and research elements.

"Under the current CLPS contract, it's all all or nothing, which might be fine if you're only doing one or two of those [missions] per year," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Space.com during a press conference on Saturday. "But when you're trying to scale up to what we're talking about today, you want to have the flexibility to move pieces around."

NASA selected eight companies to compete for the new CLPS 2 missions under the framework: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies.

The contracts for the 10-year CLPS 2 architecture carry a combined maximum value of $10 billion, rather than $10 billion in immediately awarded missions. NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the agency's "Phase One" Moon Base objectives.

NASA is also following through on a promise Isaacman made in June, when he proposed repurposing an engineering model of the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers (essentially an Earth-based twin) as a mission-ready rover to send to the moon. That rover, called PROMISE (short for "Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration"), is a nuclear-powered robot intended to explore the lunar south pole beginning in late 2028.

The autonomous rover will carry a drill and scientific instruments to search for volatiles and water ice on the lunar surface. NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an additional $140 million option period based on performance, to deliver PROMISE to the lunar surface aboard its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander.

In addition to that contract for Blue Origin, NASA awarded six launch and orbital transportation task orders worth a total of approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program.

The missions will demonstrate commercial launch and orbital transportation capabilities, including cargo transfers between Earth and lunar orbits, navigation tests with the CAPSTONE 2 spacecraft and lunar scouting with "MoonFall" drones. Blue Origin, SpaceX and Relativity Space will provide launch support with their New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Terran R rockets, respectively.

Under a separate lunar logistics contract, NASA selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites aboard its Starship megarocket in 2028, helping to establish a future lunar communications network with spacecraft similar to the company's Starlink spacecraft.

NASA also awarded contracts to Honeybee Robotics, Redwire and Yank Technologies to develop components for a lunar power and communications tower, known as miniCAST.

The announcements support NASA's Phase One Moon Base strategy, which is scheduled to extend through 2029 and focuses on robotic exploration, infrastructure demonstrations and commercial deliveries. Phase Two, which runs from 2029 to 2032, will continue to build out infrastructure for the base, which will get up and running during Phase 3.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#823. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle United, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.

#822. Lily Tomlin Reveals Dolly Parton’s Surprising 9 to 5 Preparation

Lily Tomlin exclusively shared with E! News what she remembered most from working with the late Dolly Parton on 1980's 9 to 5: "She hit with all chargers blazing."

Lily Tomlin will always love her time with Dolly Parton.

Over two months after the country legend died at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer, Tomlin shared what it was like for her and Jane Fonda to costar with Parton on 9 to 5—especially when it came to how the Grammy winner prepared for her role in the 1980 comedy.

“She came on the set, she'd memorized the whole script because she thought she was supposed to, and she hit with all chargers blazing,” Tomlin told E! News’ Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview. “Jane and I looked at each other, ‘Dolly is so great.’ And she was. She was great.”

The Grace & Frankie alum—who was joined by friend and Laugh-In creator George Schlatter for the interview—also expressed how grateful she was to have Parton as a friend for so many years, describing what being so close to the “Jolene” singer meant to her.

“It meant the innocence that was totally Dolly,” Tomlin raved. “The absolute perfection that she brought to her look—her everything.”

“That was like out of the genesis of something brilliantly thought out and wholesome, because she was that person,” the 87-year-old continued. “She just delivered the essence of that to the audience.”

As Tomlin mused, it was a feat only Parton could have achieved, quipping that while Parton was “extremely well endowed,” she managed to also be “totally innocent.”

Tomlin added, “You could totally see the innocence in her.”

Of course, her friendship with Parton wasn’t the only Hollywood relationship the Oscar nominee cultivated over the years, as she’s still very close with Schlatter over 50 years after starring on Laugh-In. Their relationship is one she speaks of fondly in the upcoming documentary Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter, which will be available to rent or buy on all digital platforms beginning Dec. 8.

And for his part, Schlatter is grateful to have cast Tomlin all those years ago.

#821. How 'Barca way' continues despite big-name exits

Esmee Brugts has made more than 100 appearances for Barcelona after joining in 2023

Barcelona's team is markedly different to the one Arsenal faced in the 2025 Women's Champions League final - but the challenge is as difficult as ever.

Three-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas was among a number of high-profile summer departures, but Barca remain favourites to continue their European domination.

The reigning champions have won all three league-phase matches, scoring 19 goals, and welcome Arsenal to the Nou Camp on Thursday (17:45 GMT).

Two seasons ago, Arsenal stunned Barcelona in the Women's Champions League final, less than five months after Renee Slegers was named permanent manager.

That victory kick-started a new era for the Gunners under Slegers, but it has not gone to plan so far this season.

Disappointing results and a five-game winless run, which ended in October, have left Arsenal sixth in the Women's Super League.

However, the Gunners have started the European campaign well and are fifth in the table with seven points from their first three matches.

And given Barcelona's summer changes, Arsenal might have hoped to be facing a team in transition - but the Spanish giants look as strong as ever.

So how have Barca - who have won four of the past six Women's Champions League titles - hit the ground running this term despite losing some of their key players?

Nations League draw, BBC Womenâs Footballer of the Year & can Arsenal shock Barcelona again?

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

What is the Women's Champions League prize money?

When Spain great Putellas left Barcelona in the summer to join London City Lionesses, it felt like the end of an era.

She was followed to Bromley by defender Mapi Leon, while full-back Ona Batlle joined Arsenal and Salma Paralluelo swapped Barcelona for European rivals Lyon.

All four had played a key part in Barcelona's dominance and ended their time at the club with a historic quadruple, including a fourth Champions League last season.

So how have Barcelona coped with losing such big players?

"Every season is different. There are always changes but we know that's football," Barcelona's Esmee Brugts told BBC Sport.

"There's an opportunity to make a new story and that's up to us. So far, I've been quite happy with how it's going.

"I'm excited for the upcoming games to see how we do. It can be a bit different - but different in a good way also."

Barcelona's success is down to multiple factors, but it all centres around a distinctive playing identity that is ingrained in Spanish footballers from a young age.

Stars such as three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati were developed at the club's famous La Masia youth academy, situated next to the Estadi Johan Cruyff, which is named after one of Barca's greatest footballers.

They produce a conveyor belt of talent, all trained to play the same way, and having learned to swap in and out of positions seamlessly.

It is a way of playing that Netherlands international Brugts has picked up with ease since joining in 2023.

"It's difficult to explain because it's so many small things. It's doing the simple things good," said Brugts. "It's a team sport. If everybody does their own roles, you'll perform the best way.

"I watched a documentary about Johan Cruyff and it's exactly how he wanted to play. It's how we try to play every week. We try to be as perfect as possible.

"We try to win every trophy there is by playing really beautiful football, in my opinion. The 'tiki-taka' I enjoy so much."

Barcelona beat rivals Real Madrid 7-0 last month in Liga F

Arsenal boss Slegers said Barcelona have "a really strong identity" and she does not believe this changes when new players come into the side.

"They can play in different positions and also have a very strong and clear way of playing. It's very impressive with the way Barcelona plays," said Slegers.

"With new players coming in and then rotating, their style of play stands up. We think we have quite a clear idea of what that could look like."

While it is a new era for Barcelona, their ambitions remain the same - to defend their four titles this season.

Brugts said they are "really building" their identity with new players in the squad and believe there are "no limits" to what they can produce.

Talented youngsters such as midfielder Clara Serrajordi, 18, defender Renee van Asten, 20, and forward Vicky Lopez, 20, have added more depth to the squad.

"It took me some time to adjust, to learn and understand what it is to play the Barca way. I'm still not there, but it's a process," said 23-year-old Brugts.

"It's an interesting journey - to do it surrounded by the best players, some that have left and some that are still here.

"I'm super-grateful and I'm super-proud if I look at what's coming up from the younger teams. I'm very impressed with how good they are.

"The way Barcelona plays is something you have to learn when you are young. Whenever we need them, they are ready to play and understand the game."

#820. Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage and in advanced talks to appoint Thomas Frank

Sage goes after 16 games with club bottom of table

He is the favourite to take over at former club Lens

Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games, with Thomas Frank in advanced talks to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League. Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford. It is hoped that he will take charge before next Saturday’s trip to Coventry.

The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening but negotiations over compensation for the rest of his three-year contract delayed his exit. A further complication was that Sage has emerged as the favourite to take over at his previous club, Lens, after they sacked Yannick Cahuzac on Tuesday. The Lens owner and president, Joseph Oughourlian, has remained in close contact with Sage and is understood to have held talks about a return. That would mean Palace could avoid paying some compensation to Sage, having spent more than £4m to buy him out of his contract when he replaced Oliver Glasner in the summer.

Palace, who confirmed that Sage’s backroom staff would also depart, said in a statement: “The club would like to place on record its thanks to Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in south London, and wish them well for the future. An update on the process of appointing a new manager will be provided in due course.”

Sunday’s defeat was Palace’s fifth in an eight-match run that also included a painful 5-0 hammering by their arch-rivals Brighton. Their only victory in the sequence came in the Carabao Cup at Fulham and they have lost four league fixtures in a row.

Palace have seven points from 10 games, their league victories having come against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, and have conceded the most goals in the division: 24. They have been juggling domestic matches with the Europa League, where they sit 21st in the 36-team table.

Sage signed a three-year contract after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season.

Alternatives to Frank include the former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche, who also has his backers at Palace, and Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager.

Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, the winger Malick Fofana.

Sage is understood to have fallen out with the board over their failure to sign what he regarded as adequate replacements for Guéhi and Lacroix. The Palace chair, Steve Parish, was unhappy with Sage’s treatment of Jaydee Canvot, another centre-back, after the France Under-21 international was dropped from the squad for September’s home defeat by Ipswich, and expressed displeasure after Adam Wharton was substituted in that match.

Thanks to a combination of radar, infrasound, dash-cam and security camera footage, astronomers have tracked the bright daytime meteor that fell over Cape Cod Bay in May 2026 back to its origin as a small asteroid perturbed by Jupiter and sent on a comet-like orbit towards Earth.

Meteor fireballs visible in the daytime are referred to as 'bolides'. At 1:06 p.m. local time (18:06 UTC) on May 30, 2026 one such bolide was widely witnessed falling out of the sky over coastal Massachusetts, with members of the public also reporting an associated sonic boom that rumbled across the north-eastern coast of the United States.

Now, a team of scientists from Europe and the United States, led by space physicist Juha Vierinen of the Arctic University of Norway in Tromsø, have patched together measurements from a meteor-observing radar network, regular weather radar, infrasound stations and camera footage to fully characterize the fall of this meteoroid and trace its orbit around the sun.

Key to these observations were measurements by the Spread Spectrum Interferometric Meteor Observing Network (SIMONe) based at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT's) Haystack Observatory. SIMONe is a project jointly developed by MIT, the Arctic University of Norway and the Leibniz Institute of Atmospheric Physics in Kühlungsborn, Germany.

"We were fortunate that the event occurred within the coverage of SIMONe," Vierinen told Space.com.

This is echoed by Ryan Volz, a radio scientist at Haystack Observatory who is a member of the team who studied the May 30 bolide. "We got pretty lucky to observe this one," Volz told Space.com. "A bolide like this would have to enter the atmosphere within about 62 miles (100 kilometers) of a SIMONe-like meteor radar system for the head echoes we saw to be detectable, and there are only a handful of places in the world that currently meet that criteria."

A head echo is what radar sees when a meteoroid – what we call the lump of rock that becomes a meteor while it is still in space – enters Earth's atmosphere, generating a cloud of plasma around it as it superheats the atmosphere and its outer surface.

"The head echoes give the best constraints on the meteoroid's trajectory," said Volz.

The existence of the head echo is usually very brief, taking place at 56 miles (90 kilometers () altitude down to about 44 miles (71 kilometers) when the plasma around the meteoroid is dense enough to return a radar echo. The head echo transitions into a 'trail echo', which is produced by a streak of turbulent plasma that is left in the wake of the meteoroid after it has passed through a given part of the atmosphere.

In the case of the 30 May bolide, the trail echo was detected down to an unusually low altitude of 20 miles (32 kilometers), at which point the falling rock fragmented with an explosive force equivalent to 500 tons of TNT, whereas the total impact energy of the bolide was in the region on 1.1 kilotons of TNT. Only three recorded bolides around the world had a greater impact energy in the year before (2025), giving an indication of how rare such events are.

At this point, four of the Next Generation Weather Radars (NEXRAD) jointly operated by the National Weather Service, the Federal Aviation Administration and the U.S. Air Force took over, recording the debris from the fragmentation as solid chunks of rock fell as meteorites into Cape Cod Bay.

The radar detections were supported by infrasound readings of the atmospheric pressure waves resulting from the hypervelocity fall and break-up of the object. These pressure waves can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometers and were picked up by the Elginfield Infrasound Array (ELFO) in Ontario, Canada, as well as by citizen scientists operating their own Raspberry Shake/Boom pressure sensors, which are build-your-own micro-barometers produced by the Raspberry Pi Foundation.

"Six citizen-operated sensors jointly constrained the arrival direction," said Vierinen. "Five other single-station detections and ELFO supplied the signal periods used to estimate the energy release. We are grateful to the citizen scientists whose measurements expanded the coverage and helped locate the event."

From the data gathered, the team were able to deduce certain properties about the object that fell to Earth over Massachusetts. The meteoroid that entered the atmosphere was about a meter (approximately three feet) across, and based on how deep it penetrated into the atmosphere before fragmenting it must have been a pretty solid body, possibly rich in iron.

"We cannot determine its exact history, but we found no association with any known meteor shower," said Vierinen.

Extrapolating its trajectory back into space, the team found that the meteoroid had a comet-like elongated orbit around the sun that took it almost as far out as Jupiter. Comets on such orbits are referred to as Jupiter-family comets, since their orbits are governed by perturbations from Jupiter's powerful gravitational influence.

However, the meteoroid was definitely not a comet, and previous research has found that Jupiter can draw out small asteroids from the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter and place them on such orbits.

"Meteoroids can be perturbed by other bodies including Jupiter," team-member Marc Fries told Space.com. "The meteoroid's aphelion – the point where it is farthest from the sun – is close to Jupiter's orbit, which suggests a close pass by the gas giant may have indeed flung it into its recent Earth-crossing path. This same process has slowly depopulated the asteroid belt throughout the solar system's history."

Meteoroids on meter-sized scales are in something of a black spot – they are not very easy to detect in space from Earth unlike larger asteroids, and they are not common enough to be falling to Earth all the time unlike the pebble-sized meteoroids and smaller that burn up as shooting stars. As such, we know relatively little about this population of bodies and every bolide that we see helps us to learn more.

"Every new piece of data we glean about Earth impactors adds to the statistics," said Fries. "It is especially helpful to have measurements of total power, location, originating orbit and similar data points for the more massive meteorites, because those are the meteoroids and asteroids we encounter less frequently."

That the meteoroid fell over such a highly populated area was a stroke of luck. Although the atmosphere is carefully monitored on a global basis by both ground stations and satellites high above us, meaning that even if a meteor streaks above an uninhabited area there is usually enough data to narrow down its trajectory somewhat, radar observations are able to do so more accurately.

"We would love to have global coverage with meteor radar networks and we and others are making progress with SIMONe and similar systems, but the current coverage is still sparse," said Volz.

Nevertheless, the Cape Cod bolide resoundingly shows that by combining radar echoes from head and trail plasma with weather radar observations and ultrasound pulses from the break-up of falling rocks, scientists can ascertain the orbits of impacting meteoroids very accurately.

While the Cape Cod meteoroid was much smaller than the asteroid that exploded over Chelyabinsk in 2013, which was about 18 meters across and exploded with an energy equivalent to between 400 and 500 kilotons of TNT, being able to trace meteoroids back to their orbits may in future reveal new populations of potentially hazardous impactors.

The research into the Cape Cod bolide is available as a preprint on the arXiv server.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#818. Young duo at heart of Nations League's meanest defence

Northern Ireland play Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday before travelling to Budapest to face Hungary on Tuesday

Across his two spells as Northern Ireland boss, Michael O'Neill has been blessed with no shortage of centre-back talent.

Jonny Evans, Aaron Hughes, Gareth McAuley and Craig Cathcart were mainstays of his first stint in charge - so much so that, in some of the biggest games of O'Neill's managerial career at Euro 2016, the quartet all started across a flat back-four.

Since returning to the job four years ago, O'Neill has switched to three at the back, with Sunderland duo Trai Hume and Dan Ballard providing an injection of Premier League quality in what remains a side largely drawn from the Championship and League One.

But with Hume, something of a Swiss army knife in the squad, covering the injured Conor Bradley on the right flank and even starting in centre midfield against Ukraine last month, and Ballard presently nursing an injured hamstring, change has been required through this Nations League campaign.

Despite those forced alterations in defence, the side go into their concluding Group B2 fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary top of their pool and the only side at any level of the competition yet to concede a goal.

At the heart of their defensive efforts have been Ruairi McConville and Tom Atcheson, two young centre-backs already described by their international manager as having "no ceiling".

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

At 21-years-old, Norwich City's McConville is the more senior of the pair.

Having been given his debut off the bench at home to Belarus two years ago this week, among the former Brighton man's early international assignments was trying to keep a rampant Alexander Isak in check during a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

In the short time since he has looked an increasingly commanding figure, leading this Nations League group in clearances made with both head and boot.

"It would be unbelievable to keep that record for these last two games and go the whole of the campaign," he said of what is Northern Ireland's longest run without conceding a goal since 2017.

McConville notes that the streak is a team effort and product of collective work-rate, rather than just the defensive three alone.

"We're a team that works hard, a team that doesn't want to give anything up.

"We're confident in ourselves and we know that we're a good side."

It is McConville who has taken on the Ballard role in the middle of the defence for the past three games, with Atcheson on the right and Oxford United's Ciaron Brown, himself superb through the campaign so far, playing from the left.

On the developing understanding between an emerging unit, McConville added: "We're enjoying playing together.

"It's still early days together and we have to keep taking it game by game and doing what the gaffer tells us and the work on the training pitch.

"We don't have much time together when we're here [in international camp] so it's important to do all we can."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Atcheson's comfort on the ball has been an asset across his six caps

After 16 caps, McConville is a relative veteran compared to Atcheson, who made his international bow in a friendly against Wales in March at a time when he had only four senior club starts to his name at Blackburn Rovers.

The most recent of those had come under O'Neill, then in a short stint as caretaker manager at the Championship club.

Clearly impressed by what he saw from the now 20-year-old at Ewood Park, Atcheson made his first Northern Ireland start against Guinea in June, a game in which he scored the winner with a fabulous flick before later being shown a red card.

Some 428 minutes into his international career, Atcheson is still to experience what it feels like to concede a goal.

The England-born defender feels Ballard "is definitely a big miss" to the side, but believes the squad's understanding of O'Neill's desired system is an asset to those who have starred during the Sunderland man's latest absence.

"I feel like everyone knows what they need to do, everyone knows their job, the details of the formation we play and system," he said.

"That's so key and I think that's why we're so solid defensively.

"It's a team thing, we're set up right, we're very on it all the time and everyone gives their all."

#817. Carrick sacked by Manchester United with team in Premier League relegation zone – live

⚽️ Head coach departs after one win in 11 games ⚽️ Carrick was latest fall guy for dysfunctional hierarchy ⚽️ Have any thoughts? Email John

Michael Carrick has been dismissed by Manchester United. He departs after a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford last Sunday that left the team in the Premier League’s bottom three. United twice fought back from two goals down for a late point against Villa, after a dramatic recovery to defeat Roma in the Champions League five days earlier, but that wasn’t enough.

United are third-bottom in the Premier League, a point behind 17th-placed Coventry, and 17th in the Champions League league phase table. His departure follows a review led by the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.

David Flynn gets in touch: “Hi John, I must say I don’t fully agree that United keep appointing yesterday’s men, they’ve also tried appointing tomorrow’s men (Amorin, Ten Haag) and nobody’s men (Carrick, Ole). It’s actually a broad spectrum of mistakes that they keep making.”

Ben Monroe-Lake gets in touch: “We live in an age of incredibly powerful individuals, people who wield vast amounts of money and influence and increasingly make little attempt to hide how readily they are to fling such influence and money around for their own benefit. Trump, Musk, Huang, Zuckerberg etc.

“And yet at the same time, these people seem entirely unable to not show everyone their arse, on ever more impressive stages, in ever more shocking ways. So the mind trust at Manchester United are a particularly great microcosm of this. Men of a particular age, who voluntarily took up this position, wrested control of the football operations in fact, as they thought they could do it better. Yet it’s obvious how bad they are at this, even without seeing inside their Monaco based boardrooms.

“Extend Ten Hag’s contract based on the performance in one game. Force in a young manager with a rigid tactical plan without the players to support it. Fire the person you paid Newcastle Utd a huge fee to hire, because he points out this is stupid. Keep on the interim manager with little experience and don’t fill the most gaping holes in his squad.

“In between this, fire the tea ladies, make some questionable pronouncements and who can even remember all the gaffes.

“Of course it’s slightly terrifying that people who are essentially “in charge” are so stupid but it’s a little bit mollifying that people that seem happy to wade waist deep into all aspects of our lives are as dumb as I am. All that really separates me from them is luck and being more willing to get up at five in the morning. So perhaps one day someone not a total bozo will make enough money to buy a football club.”

David Wall gets in touch: “One thing that concerns me about Pochettino is how he will engage with the academy. There was a lot made when he was at Spurs about how he favoured young players. But in fact most of those young players were bought in from outside of the club. It was only Kane from their academy who became a regular in the first team (perhaps with Winks, although more as a squad player rather than first choice). Is Pochettino the type of manager who will spend his midweek evenings going to watch the youth sides play, or is he just going to give an instruction about age-profile to the recruitment department?”

Winks started the 2019 Champions League final, as did Kane, rather unfortunately. At Chelsea, there was definite friction with the club hierarchy, though the signs at United are that he could have the personality to create his own powerbase. Within United, there is a great big vacuum that someone needs to fill.

The problem with Pochettino is that he’s very much the face of 2015 rather than 2026, setting aside what was a decent enough USMNT World Cup until it all went wrong. United keep doing this. Louis van Gaal would have been a fine appointment in 1996 rather than 2015, and Jose Mourinho would have been ideal in 2003, rather than 2016. Of course, United had a good manager in those days but times move on.

Joe Taylor gets in touch: “Spurs fan here. I’m a bit confused by the Pochettino-Spurs revisionism. Sometimes managers don’t get credit for taking players that until that point hasn’t achieved anything and turning them into world beaters (eg. Eriksen, Son) but in this case he doesn’t even get credit for players that didn’t do anything before or after his tenure (eg. Dier, Dele Alli, Dembele, Lamela). I’d suggest he had quite a large hand in that squad that supposedly made his life easy. I think he’s perfect for United right now.”

I’d agree. He made the most of what he had, and a player of a couple of players who have achieved very little without his help. There’s a few projects to work on at United.

Warning: Poch may not be an instant cure for the Manchester United malaise.

At Chelsea, just one win from his first six league games, same at Southampton and Espanyol, while at Tottenham he won two and drew two. At PSG, he won four of his first six games, which at that club is probably below par.

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) earlier issued a statement following Carrick’s dismissal pinning the blame for poor results firmly on the ownership. In full below:

double quotation markMichael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager.

The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.

But the discontent at United is not just about matters on the pitch. Far from it.

Aggressive ticketing policies have further damaged relations with supporters. Treating loyal fans principally as a source of revenue undermines their identity and the bond with the team that sustains support through difficult times. Supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights.

The earlier Stretford End banner declaring “The way you treat us is a disgrace” was a warning. The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.

MUST warned publicly in January 2025 that alienating supporters risked a downward spiral of worsening atmosphere, performances and financial outcomes. Our subsequent Telegraph article urged Sir Jim Ratcliffe to break that “doom loop” by bringing supporters with him. Those warnings remain painfully relevant.

The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success. Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.

The pattern is repeated, the problems remain the same. Wrote this a couple of weeks ago.

double quotation markBeyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

And with that I shall hand over to John Brewin for the afternoon session.

An email! “I’m a lifelong Spurs fan and enjoyed having Poch as manager,” writes Alan. “But he did have a squad that made his life pretty easy. By the start of his second season, 2015-16, he could field this side: Lloris; Walker, Alderweireld, Vertonghen, Rose; Eriksen, Dier, Dembele; Dele Alli, Kane, Son. Not sure how many of the current United squad would get into that team. Sadly most of them would also get into the current Spurs team!”

The timing of Pochettino’s expected arrival will be interesting. The US men’s side have a Concacaf Nations League game against Haiti in Kingston, Jamaica, on Saturday, with the return leg next Wednesday in Cincinnati. Manchester United travel to Anfield in the Premier League four days later.

The nitty gritty of that is surely forming part of the conversations ongoing now. Either way, US Soccer will be quids-in as Jeff Rueter explains here.

double quotation markThe real boon is his release clause, a reported $10m (£7.5m) option that only a Big Club could afford to spring. Had Pochettino left after the World Cup, coach and federation would have parted with nothing more exchanged than a handshake and some pleasantries. Instead, they forged an insurance policy to make up for what could have been if Pochettino had stayed for a full cycle.

A few comments from below the line on our news story.

Impossible job and yet he still finished third. This is the weakest squad Utd have had in 40 years. That’s not Michael’s fault. He can walk either his head held high. The fish rots from the head and it’s spread right thru the Utd body. Michael got caught up in it, bloody useless players in the main.

Pochettino flatters to decieve, won nothing at Tottenham, PSG are better under Luis Enrique and USA much of a muchness, it'll be another round of we made mistakes yet again at United inside 18 months. And Carrick was treated appallingly by the hierarchy, Relegation would be just desserts.

Thank you Michael. Your conduct was exemplary. Once it became known that WIlcox leads a review, it was clear he would recommend Ratcliffe to fire Carrick. Otherwise he would be to blamed himself. How come the club that was 3rd last year is 3rd from bottom this year, with the same coach? The obvious answer is that recruitment failed. Wilcox can't have that, so better blame coach. I think one of the problems of United and hierarchy is that they are opportunistic in their managerial appointments. Not only they don't have a long-term strategy, they don't even have a short-term strategy and fire coaches when other options they identify previously become available. They fired van Gaal because they contacted Mourinho, they pursued Amorim, now they fire Carrick when they are able to get a deal with Pochettino.

Do yourself a favour and read Barney Ronay’s piece on Poch’s imminent arrival. These lines feel particularly apt:

double quotation markHow do you solve a club that has won two major trophies in 10 years of steady downward progress? Easy. You hire a coach who has also won two major trophies in 13 years of steady downward progress. How do we get back to the dimly remembered recent past? We hire the dimly remembered recent past.

Does this feel like a magic bullet? At this stage hiring Pochettino is like booking the bloke who did Gangnam Style to play the Super Bowl. Yeah, huge fan. Remind me. Weren’t you quite big in 2013?

What next for Michael Carrick is also an interesting question. Has he done enough to put himself in contention for the next Premier League vacancy that comes up? Or is it back to the Championship, where his tenure with Middlesbrough was mixed to say the least? With Regis Le Bris and Matthias Jaissle probably looking the least secure in the top flight at the moment, might a return to the north east be on the cards at some point for the Wallsend-born man? Doesn’t feel quite right, does it? But you never know.

Hello all. Perhaps the most immediate problem facing Mauricio Pochettino when he arrives will be playing personnel. It’s painfully obvious – and is has been for years – that where once Manchester United was home for the best of the best, these days it’s … not. Everyone has their own view on players but when you look at the teamsheets for the key recent games against Aston Villa, Chelsea and, yes, Bournemouth you’d be hard-pressed to suggest that United had a truly superior 20-man matchday squad for those games. And Pochettino isn’t going to be able to fix that overnight.

John Ashdown is here to take the blogging reins.

You have to credit Manchester United. Your local rivals have turned the Premier League into an almost meaningless farce. We are questioning the validity of anything we’ve seen over the past 20 years; wondering how many goals Erling Haaland will get in the Championship. We are looking at the league table from second position down and wishing we’d invested in inflatable bananas a month ago.

And yet here comes the Old Trafford machine: from players to the captain to the manager to the director of football, to the director of the director of football, to a minority owner who feels the UK is being “colonised by immigrants”, to debt-leveraging majority owners who take vast sums out of the club and are collectively saying hold my Ineos-sponsored high-performance wellness immune boost smoothie.

Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article. Read this and compare and contrast. From 11 August 2022: “Reds rinse and repeat: will we ever break the Manchester United crisis cycle?” There are others.

“Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article,” as Max Rushden wrote recently. Another piece that’s well worth revisiting …

Here’s a data graphic on how Manchester United, under Carrick, went from good last season to bad this season.

“Michael Carrick has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. There is almost total agreement on the latter point, that United’s issues are structural and systemic and absolve Carrick of blame. Still, he’s gotta go, because what can you do, eh?”

“Pochettino who built something at Tottenham despite the environment,” Daniel writes of the Argentinian in that piece below “… the sense is that, as when Mourinho arrived at Old Trafford after years of speculation, he’s past his magical best.”

In January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.

The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish to some of the worst football in their history.

It is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, his l’état, c’est moi mentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.

Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games. The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League.

Thomas Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

“Sadness it’s come to this … more sadness because it’s Michael,” Gary Neville tells Sky Sports News. “I wish he hadn’t got the job at the end of the season … I didn’t expect it to happen this quickly, but it is what it is … the position in the league is terrible [but] the club is spinning on a roundabout again.

“It’s a really poor reflection on the decision-makers. To get the ending right [with a manager] is very difficult … it can be clumsy … I think I said after the Bournemouth game, Manchester United effectively watched Carrick resign on the pitch, that wave goodbye.

“Indecision … lack of authority … poor leadership [from the club hierarchy] … in the last 24, 48 hours, it’s been spectacularly bad … to be in Monaco while your manager is taking training, while also approaching Mauricio Pochettino …

“Quite simply disgusting … in any other industry, it would be constructive dismissal, and you’d be getting sued … I don’t think anybody comes out of this well at all.

“[European] Super League was the ultimate low, a betrayal of the English game … I think this is a low, but you don’t even get angry anymore … you just feel, like, nothing … it makes you numb, I think the fans are sick of it, I think everyone is sick of it.”

“I have been a supporter for 60 years,” emails Graham. “I hope we get relegated, lose lots of money and get rid of the owners. Only in this way will we ever get back to being a club that supporters are truly connected with and are proud of.”

“Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.”

Coming up next: must-read analysis on Carrick’s departure from Jamie Jackson.

“In my 53 years supporting United this is most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years,” emails Robert.

“The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they seeing winning as a nice to have, not the core objective of an elite football club.

“Pretty much every club in Premier League is run and managed better than United. And this is why the decline of the club that started with the Glazers taking ownership is now reaching its terminal point.

“I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. And it was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail, and fail quickly.

“Our first-team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us?

“It really doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue. Relegation might be what we need.”

“Are we a bit late to the party with Pochettino?” wonders Paul Scholes on The Good, The Bad & The Football podcast.

“I actually think he’s a brilliant appointment ... he could be perfect ... but I’ve got that slight concern we are not getting his best years.”

Manchester United’s owners, rather than Michael Carrick, are to blame for the club’s problems, a fans’ group has said.

“Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United,” said a statement from the Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST).

“We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

“The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager.

“They lie with the ownership. The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When Ineos came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

“It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.” Press Association

“I disagree with the earlier comment that Carrick is not to blame in some way,” emails Ryan.

“He presided over apparently a poor pre-season program as the players look unfit v other sides in the league, he continues to play Dalot at left-back rather than use someone from the academy, and his tactics overall have been muddled. Of course the board bear a lot of the blame, because the signings weren’t delivered, but he has made the situation worse.”

After Nottingham Forest 3-1 Manchester City, meanwhile, will Pochettino be appointing a second-ball coach?

Personally I don’t think it would be a bad idea:

As Mauricio Pochettino left the podium to close his final press conference of the last international window, he offered an ambiguous farewell.

“See you next …” Pochettino began as he headed to the tunnels of Allianz Field in Saint Paul, before cutting his sentence short. Then, a bit of a sing-song: “See you next, see you next.”

You don’t need an AI clanker’s autocomplete function to try closing the sentence. “See you next month” would have been synonymous with “see you next window”, after all. Still, the farewell felt poignant given questions about whether Pochettino was going to last a full four-year cycle as US men’s national team head coach.

Jamie Jackson exclusively revealed on Monday night that Manchester United were about to press the “Sack Carrick” button:

“Is Pochettino actually a good manager?” ponders Jon on email.

“He did well at Spurs - albeit without winning anything - and in a short spell at Southampton but that was a long time ago. Since then his record has been pretty underwhelming, up to and including an uninspiring time in charge of the US men’s team. He just seems to have a reputation as a good manager but I’m not really sure what it’s based on anymore.”

“And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

“But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?”

“This feels sadder than every other time it’s happened since Ferguson retired,” emails John. “Each of the previous managers had to go, as in large part the underperformance very much felt like it was their fault. This doesn’t feel like that. It was so astoundingly obvious we needed another striker and left back in the summer, and we’ve suffered hugely (and immediately) because neither were brought in.

“Carrick has been left with a dire situation and whereas with the others (Amorim: change formation; ETH: play Casemiro; Moyes: stop crossing 80 times per game and so on and so on), as a fan I can’t look at our performances and think of an obvious error. But, because the owners and exec aren’t going to sack themselves, and because you can’t fire the players, you change the only thing you can ... the manager. And then repeat the cycle all over again.”

While Andy emails: “Carrick isn’t the story. Pochettino isn’t the story. The Glazer family is the story. Manchester City has been ruined by corruption and Manchester United has been ruined by debt and mismanagement. The pressure for the owners to sell up needs to be taken up to a new level. That’s it.”

Gary Neville has called Manchester United “classless” over their actions in the days before Carrick’s sacking.

The manager’s departure was announced on Thursday and Mauricio Pochettino has been lined up to replace him.

Confirmation of Carrick’s sacking came after a period of limbo for the former midfielder, who reported to Carrington on Thursday after taking training on Tuesday and Wednesday.

His fate was sealed the day after a meeting in Monaco, when director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada travelled to see co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Speaking on the Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast, recorded prior to Thursday’s confirmation, Neville said the process feels “clumsy”.

“We’re sat here today recording this programme knowing that Michael Carrick is going to be sacked tomorrow, knowing that they’re speaking to Mauricio Pochettino … But I think the fact they’re in Monaco now and they can’t sack him today knowing that it’s happening, to me it just feels a little bit clumsy, it feels a little bit classless.

“I think if you live in Monaco, you can’t leave a guy hanging for 24 or 48 hours just because you live in Monaco, that can’t happen.” Press Association

“Wilcox, Berada and Ratcliffe should have fired themselves,” emails Deb, a “long-suffering Mancunian.”

“They are the common denominator of all this failure. Poch will last 12 months if he’s lucky. What a shower …”

2009-2012 Espanyol 2013-2014 Southampton 2014-2019 Tottenham 2021-2022 Paris Saint-Germain 2023-2024 Chelsea 2024-2026 USMNT

Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Manchester United’s next fixture is the small matter of a Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield, Sunday 22 November: kick-off 4.30pm.

Then on Wednesday 25 November, it’s a date with Sporting in Lisbon in the Champions League.

On Saturday, 28 November, it’s a 3pm kick-off against Brentford in the Premier League.

“After going through the Moyes season,” writes Hugh, “the dross football of Mourinho and Van Gaal, the moments-years of Solskjaer, the Rangnick surgery that never was, the middling Ten Hag, the baffling Amorim, and now a decent man thrust into the meat grinder, this is the first year it’s been genuinely hard to watch Man Utd with any emotion.

“And it’s not because of the football. It’s that the Glazer ownership and Ratcliffe mismanagement has met the Man City revelations, meaning it’s hard to see the point anymore. £1bn taken out of the club while others were illicitly pumping in roughly the same. A club drained of life, hollowed out … I can take crap football, but I can’t take this anymore.”

“I think it was Jonathan Liew who made the eminently sensible suggestion of a positional switch (not so rare in football) for Michael Carrick - by having him replace Jason Wilcox as director of football,” emails Geoff.

“Just waiting for Mr Mediocrity Wilcox to do the honorable thing and admit he is out of his depth and responsible in part for the situation and resign. The golf course and the pundit circuit call … Michael, you will always be welcomed back into the crowd by all United fans.”

Clearly, there is sadness and regret within the club that Carrick has been dismissed. But the run of one win in 10 Premier League games was seen as unacceptable “by any measure” – and there is a belief that a different manager will get more from the squad. Performances and results in the last three games – the 2-0 defeat by Chelsea, a stirring 3-2 win against Roma and the 4-4 draw with Villa – were not enough to convince the club hierarchy that they were on the right path.

“As a United fan who was around for the early 90s and the many successes that followed, seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation,” emails Chris. “He was the only likeable thing about a club and set of players who I find it harder to support as I get older.

“I’ve lived and understood all the schadenfreude that goes with United failing over the last 13 years and I get it, but frankly I’m finding it hard to invest the emotional energy in the team any more. I took my eight-year-old lad to Old Trafford for the Brighton game in the FA Cup in January, and I’ve never experienced a more toxic atmosphere at a football ground.

“The fans - and I mean the locals, the ones who go to games, who can remember the days before Ronaldo - we deserve better ... better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment.

“It’s harder and harder to find the hope that should accompany the appointment of a new manager but what other choice do we have?”

The former Burnley, QPR and Southampton goal machine Charlie Austin is in the pundit’s chair on Sky Sports News right now. He says United have to clear the decks – let Mauricio Pochettino rebuild completely. Which is fair, although it’s not like there will be unlimited funds.

“Allow him to work from the bottom up,” Austin says of the incoming Argentinian gaffer.

“If they don’t do that, we’ll be in the same scenario in 18 months’ time.”

“Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.”

Barney Ronay, there, writing a few days ago.

Here is the statement from the club now published on the official website:

“Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

Manchester United have sacked Michael Carrick as their head coach with the team in the Premier League’s relegation zone and lined up Mauricio Pochettino to take over.

Pochettino has a framework agreement to join a club who have one win from their past 11 matches. The USA head coach, a Premier League manager with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea, has a release clause of about $10m (£7.5m). United will have to pay more to take his staff.

Michael Carrick has been dismissed by Manchester United. He departs after a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford last Sunday that left the team in the Premier League’s bottom three. United twice fought back from two goals down for a late point against Villa, after a dramatic recovery to defeat Roma in the Champions League five days earlier, but that wasn’t enough.

United are third-bottom in the Premier League, a point behind 17th-placed Coventry, and 17th in the Champions League league phase table. His departure follows a review led by the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.
