#756. Sacha Gervasi’s ‘Darlington’ Is a Tech Billionaire Film Unlike All the Others

With one of the most impressive casts of any AFM project, Gervasi’s Renée Zellweger, Dominic Sessa and Peter Dinklage-starring film is set to take on extortionate wealth in the least political — and most entertaining — way possible.

Sacha Gervasi knows The Terminal changed everything for him.

The British screenwriter and filmmaker was at a dinner party a couple of years before he began work on his directorial debut, a rockumentary about a Canadian metal band he’d befriended over 25 years earlier (2008’s Anvil! The Story of Anvil), when he met a “total stranger” with whom he formed an immediate bond. “I had no idea who he was, and he said, ‘Oh, I’m a screenwriter,'” Gervasi recalls to The Hollywood Reporter. “And then I looked him up, and I was like, ‘Oh my god!’ It’s like meeting Mick Jagger.” Related Stories TV Gang Dong-won, Kim Go-eun to Lead Netflix's Period Romance-Action Drama 'The Twilight Between Us' Business Long-time James Bond Producer Barbara Broccoli Named President of U.K.'s National Film and Television School

This man just so happened to be Oscar-winning industry heavyweight Steven Zaillian (Schindler’s List), who became — and remains — a mentor to Gervasi. Zaillian introduced the Brit to Steven Spielberg, a meeting that would eventually lead to his 2004 starrer with Tom Hanks playing a man stuck in New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport terminal. “It opened so many doors,” Gervasi nods. “It’s a massive thing in the life of any writer to have arguably the greatest director in the history of the medium say, ‘I want to direct your script.'” That collaboration would allow Gervasi to work on a slew of other projects, such as 2010’s Henry’s Crime, 2012’s Hitchcock, and, in 2018, his passion project My Dinner with Hervé. The Peter Dinklage-led drama followed the later days of French star Hervé Villechaize, whom Gervasi interviewed just a couple of days before his 1993 suicide.

And as brilliant as the director-writer’s anecdotes about Hanks and his years-spanning friendship with Dinklage are, it’s his latest feature that we’re here to discuss — another product of Gervasi’s deep-rooted Hollywood ties, which, he admits, can be traced back to the Stevens. “I owe them everything,” says Gervasi from his L.A. home.

In Darlington, represented by CAA for North American rights and launching international sales with Rocket Science at AFM, Kate Spencer (Renée Zellweger) is a faded television actress long-forgotten by the industry. She’s invited to reprise her most famous role — not in a revival of the show, but in the real world, where a reclusive tech billionaire (The Holdovers star Dominic Sessa) has meticulously restored an English country estate to its former glory. Having retreated from the world, he now lives his life there in the fantasy that it is actually 1923. As Kate settles into this strange, controlled existence, she discovers that illusion and reality are far more entwined than she ever imagined.

“Someone described the film as The Truman Show meets The Remains of the Day, and I think that’s pretty accurate,” Gervasi says. He was inspired to write the script based off the buzzing questions he had for current-day tech billionaires, who have more money than they know what to do with. “The idea [is] that when you can do anything, and you actually do do anything, how healthy is that for the rest of the world and the people in there?” he asks.

But unlike the more searing takes we’ve had this year on the tech billionaire — Artificial, The Social Reckoning, and Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary immediately spring to mind — Gervasi maintains this is by no means a political film. “It is light-hearted. I think there are stakes and there’s real emotion to it,” he says. “But ultimately, it’s satirical. […] It’s not a treatise on the profound meaning of tech billionaires.”

Below, Gervasi dives into the making of Darlington, set to kick off production in the U.K. in early spring. He talks about luring the hard-to-pin-down Zellweger on board, why he couldn’t resist working with Dinklage once again, and how, in an industry that’s never seen more hurdles, he got this high-concept, original story over the line.

Sacha, you began your career with a documentary…

Yeah, I wanted to direct something, having been a bit in the Hollywood system. I went to UCLA Film School and then started to get out there, and then was immensely fortunate that Steven Spielberg made a script of mine with Tom Hanks. It was an incredible thing because when I arrived in L.A., I didn’t know a single person. I knew that pitching my documentary about two elderly Canadian metal stars who no one’s heard of didn’t exactly inspire commercial excitement. Let me put it that way. So I knew that I had to do it myself. So I ended up reconnecting with a band I’d known when I was 15 and had been on the road with as a roadie. And it’s a story about the cost of refusing to give up your dreams. Because most artists don’t make it. […] You find that a lot of people give up, or others just keep going for its own sake. And there was something I felt very pure about that, and very inspiring about that. That these guys were not bitter at all; they just did what they loved, and they just didn’t give a fuck.

How did dipping your toe in the documentary waters inform the rest of your career?

Obviously, I became a writer and I’ve worked — silently — on many big films, which has been its own reward. I’m lucky for the day job, but it’s really the personal projects like Anvil… I paid for that documentary myself because no one would pay for it. So I love doing these films and I also love working with Peter Dinklage. I met Peter Dinklage in 2001, and I had this idea to do a story about Hervé Villechaize, who I’d interviewed back in the ’90s, and I was the last person to interview him. Five days later, he sadly committed suicide. […] I felt like I wanted to tell a story, and I met Peter Dinklage. I wrote it as a short, and that short actually reached Steven Spielberg, and he hired me basically because he read My Dinner with Hervé.

Well, what happened was I met a total stranger at a dinner who turned out to be Steven Zaillian, who had won the Oscar for Schindler’s List. I had no idea who he was, and he said, “Oh, I’m a screenwriter.” And then I looked him up, and I was like, “Oh my god!” It’s like meeting Mick Jagger. I gave him my demo tape and he passed it on to Steven Spielberg. So the only reason I have a career today is because of Steven Zaillian. He believed in me at a very early stage, introduced me to Steven, and that script eventually became a film. […] I love the personal films and in a way Darlington is one of those films because it’s from my life. I’ve observed a lot of the things that the film speaks to.

Just before we get on to Darlington, how did The Terminal open industry doors for you?

I mean, how did it not? It’s a massive thing in the life of any writer to have arguably the greatest director in the history of the medium say, “I want to direct your script.” It opened so many doors. […] In terms of the two Stevens, Zaillian and Spielberg, I owe them everything. Particularly Steve [Zaillian] because he was and is my mentor and is my best friend in the world.

And I can tell you one quick story, which I don’t know if I’ve told before. I was working with Tom Hanks on a project at his office and I was driving him home, and Tom said to me, “Do you mind if I take the wheel for a moment?” And I said, “Okay.” He was in the passenger seat. And I said, “Why?” And he took the wheel and said, “Well, because I’m going to be starring in your movie.” And I completely freaked out, and I was like, “What the fuck?” I put my hands on my head, and thank god Tom Hanks had the foresight to take the steering wheel. I’ve had crazy encounters like that, and he’s an extraordinary man. […] The alternative is he doesn’t take the wheel, and we both crash and die. No movie and no Tom Hanks. So I feel like it was a good choice from him.

With Darlington, you’re not only the director but the writer too, so this is a very singular vision.

It is a real personal thing. […] I sat back and I was like, okay, so I’ve done biopics about Alfred Hitchcock, about Anvil, about Hervé Villechaize, and I felt like it was time to do something different. So I think this carries with it the energy of being a different phase in my creative life. It’s not based on anything or anyone. It was just an idea I had. During COVID, I was quite isolated, like everyone was, and it was a very challenging experience. I just thought there’s this thing about loneliness and it just made me think about the world. I was watching all these the rise of the tech billionaire people, and how interesting and changed the world has become because of them — the disproportionate power they hold, and the unfairness of those types of people. This is why there’s tremendous apathy toward the ruling class because there’s this sense of total disconnection from the world. Born out of me was this idea of doing a dark comedy, a satire. For me, the idea of a young guy making billions and suddenly with the means to leave reality behind, constructing a new reality… It felt to me like we’re not far away from that. If Elon Musk announced that he’s bought a Caribbean island and he’s now living in the 16th century as a pirate, we wouldn’t be that shocked.

Just as an example. [I don’t] personally know him. But the idea [is] that when you can do anything, and you actually do do anything, how healthy is that for the rest of the world and the people in there? […] There is a lack of empathy and understanding for people who don’t have those types of resources. And just in my travels around the world, I’ve seen the blindness of incredible wealth, particularly to other human beings on the planet.

If you can do anything, then it’s very easy to forget how other human beings on the planet are impacted. So there’s a satire in there. It’s gentle. It’s not a political movie by any stretch of the imagination. It’s an entertaining kind of exploration of what it might be like if someone did something like this. Our eyes and ears are through the experiences of an actress, in this case, played by Renee Zellweger. […] So it’s just a number of things [that] came together from being in the world, through COVID and looking at how things have changed and how the balance of power and wealth has changed so substantially, and wanting to get inside that and ask a few questions, but also wanting, hopefully, an entertaining, fun movie. It is entertainment and it’s a bittersweet comedy in the vein of Hal Ashby. Through COVID, I watched all of Hal Ashby’s movies again. He’s a real touchpoint for me in terms of the quiet ludicrousness of the situation and playing straight the humor of it. You’re playing something absurd, but everyone’s taking it really seriously. There’s an element of that in Darlington. […] Someone described the film as The Truman Show meets The Remains of the Day, and I think that’s pretty accurate.

It’s funny how tech billionaires have proven to be such ripe material, even just this year alone.

Yeah. And I think we have to be real — most of the world resents them. Because some of them behave in a way that could come across as arrogant and demeaning and entitled, and it just seems generally unfair and completely out of touch with the struggles of the rest of humanity. When you’re starting your own space program, and people can’t afford to buy groceries, it does seem a little bit ridiculous. So I think there’s a natural spotlight on who these people are, what are they doing, and have they lost touch so completely with planet Earth? […] A lot of them are genuinely trying to improve the world. But there is something unusual about having billions and billions of dollars and being able to do anything. Maybe it’s not such a good thing.

It sounds to me like a little more of a light-hearted take on the tech billionaire than we’ve seen so far.

It is light-hearted. I think there are stakes and there’s real emotion to it. But ultimately, it’s satirical. It’s having fun with it. It is an entertaining audience film, hopefully a sophisticated one. It’s not a treatise on the profound meaning of tech billionaires. It’s more like, ‘These people are fucking crazy.’

She is incredible. She’s so dexterous. She’s done so many things, and I think that she really sparked, hopefully, to the originality of the idea, and we met and we got on. Renee came along at exactly the right moment, and she is absolutely perfect. I could not ask for anyone better. Her acting chops are indisputable. She’s always played interesting characters, and I think again, this is a challenge for her because she’s never quite done this before. And I think that’s one of the reasons she was kind of like, “This could be interesting for me.” […] Dominic Sessa is a great, young up-and-coming actor who I love, and Alexander [Payne], our executive producer, discovered him and put him in The Holdovers. Alexander’s involved with this film, so it was a natural fit there. And Dominic is extraordinary. I got very lucky.

Dominic is a real star in the making after Tony too.

He’s very soulful. He’s really skilled. He’s just a natural, and he’s been, so far, just a pleasure to deal with. And I love him. There’s a mother-son element to this film. I think the Renee-Dominic [dynamic], that really works. Tte thing about being a filmmaker is it’s great because if you get really good actors, as we have in this case, you just get a front-row seat to watch these incredible people be creative. My job is to just not fuck it up too much and just let them do that brilliantly. (Laughs.)

And then also Peter Dinklage, who I’ve been working with on and off since 2002 or something. Peter came to read an earlier version of this script, you know, we put together a group of actors. […] He’ll always be honest with me [and] we have an ongoing collaboration.

Is it tempting for you to say, “Peter, I’ve got a job for you…” every time you make a film?

No, no. We get together, we spoon, and we love each other. (Laughs.) No, but we’re just good friends. We’ve been in each other’s lives for so long that it just felt natural. He actually read the script when I rewrote it and he called me up and said, “I have to do this film with you. So tell me what you want.” I said, “What do you want to do?” He said, “I’ll do anything. I just don’t want to be the housemaid.” I said, “Okay, let’s rule that out.” Great actors, to me, are present, available. They’re open to things. They want to engage in readings and kind of develop stuff and Peter’s just so good at that. He helps a lot of people and he’s helped me a lot, so I feel great that I can cast him in this particular part. It’s going to be really fun. […] We forget how massive Game of Thrones was [and] he has millions of fans across the world.

And to you, he’s just your spooning partner.

It’s coming together. It’s fantastic people. Alison Owen [Ghosts, Back To Black, Me Before You], and Deb Hayward, her partner [Bridget Jones’s Baby, Les Miserable] and obviously Alexander Payne. [The Holdovers, Sideways]. Our production company has generated this project, Portobello Electric, which is me and Jim Garavente [Game Night], who is just a fantastic producer. This is the perfect model for us in terms of Portobello because we want to build our own projects, and this is one we’ve spent quite a few years putting together and getting the script right and doing readings. And before anyone’s reading it, we’ve really been through it to try and get it to a really good spot. And of course, [as] we make it, it will hopefully evolve further… [And] the business has been so heavily impacted in recent years that I find it sometimes hard to be creative in that environment. But this is why we formed the production company: so that we could have the runway to build projects like Darlington, and we have quite a few others in the pipeline.

L.A. is home, but is it exciting to have a reason to come back to the U.K. for a bit?

I don’t need a reason to come back. I love it. But yeah, look, it’s called Darlington. It’s obviously playing into that whole tradition of English country house movies, but it’s not that. England is where I was born. I love it, and the crews are the best in the world, as everyone knows. There’s a level of craftsmanship and artistry that’s second to none in Britain. So that is a huge part of the appeal, and the fact that Alison and Deb are such accomplished U.K. producers with such extraordinary films under their belts… They really know how to put this stuff together in the U.K. So we’ve got all the right people to make something special, and it seems to be falling down in the right way.

This period now, where a cast is on board and the shoot’s coming up, but you’ve still got a few months of breathing space, what emotions come up for you?

Terror. (Laughs.) Also excitement. Terrifying excitement. Because I’m just watching movies. I’m watching all those great Hal Ashby movies again. I’m watching all the reference point films. I’m thinking about certain scenes. I’m doing storyboards for certain sequences. I’m thinking about, ‘How do I make the script better?’ I’m actually doing a reading of the script in a week with some other actor friends, just to hear it with all my actors lined up in mind and make whatever adjustments.

It’s a rare privilege to be able to tell original stories, particularly in this world. And I’m extremely grateful that we’ve spent the time to get to this place, and again. When me and Peter were making Hervé, we were told to give up by one mini studio head: “It’s a suicidal dwarf movie. It’s never going to get made.” I like confounding the naysayers. I like going, “Well, okay. We did it. And we’re really happy with it.” And Peter, by his own admission, gives one of the greatest performances he’s ever given. That’s really satisfying because everyone will doubt and say no and poo-poo the ideas, but just keep going with what you believe in. It’s kind of like Anvil. […] I keep playing the songs. There’s never been more hurdles and more reasons to not do this than there is now. You just have to use that to make you stronger and more determined.

#755. Iconic first image of black hole holds up to scrutiny

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way from the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong and F. Diakogiannis/CSIRO

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration wowed the world in 2019 with the first picture ever taken of a black hole’s shadow. Some researchers were unconvinced, arguing that the circular shape seen in that shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Now, an independent group has reanalysed the EHT data, and its results, published on 11 November in Nature — including new images of the black hole — largely corroborate the original findings1.

To image black holes, the international EHT collaboration stitches together data it collects simultaneously from an array of ground-based radio telescopes that stretches across several continents. The reconstruction is extremely challenging, but in principle, the result is an image with the same level of detail, or resolution, that would be achieved with a single radio dish as wide as Earth.

Although blurry, the EHT shot of a supermassive black hole at the centre of the M87 galaxy was consistent with astrophysical models based on Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes. The image had a bright ring of roughly the correct radius, given what was known about the size of the black hole, with a darker disk at the centre.

However, starting in 2022, Junichiro Makino, an astrophysicist at Kobe University in Japan, and his collaborators began questioning those conclusions2. By applying one of the data-analysis techniques the EHT collaboration had used, but with slightly different assumptions, Makino’s team obtained a different result. Their image shows a glob of radio emissions rather than a ring.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03642-7

#754. Lashana Lynch, Paapa Essiedu, Russell Tovey Join Jury for BAFTA’s Rising Star Award Nominees

Robert Aramayo of 'I Swear' claimed last year's Rising Star honor at the BAFTA Film Awards, voted for by the public.

Lashana Lynch, Paapa Essiedu and Russell Tovey have joined the panel of industry heavyweights deciding the next batch of EE BAFTA Film Awards Rising Star nominees.

The winner, voted for by the public, will pick up the honor at the Film Awards ceremony on Feb. 21. Past recipients include David Jonsson, Mia McKenna-Bruce, Letitia Wright, James McAvoy, Eva Green, Daniel Kaluuya, Kristen Stewart, Tom Hardy, Emma Mackey, Lynch herself, and, most recently, I Swear‘s Robert Aramayo.

Lynch is best known for roles in The Day of the Jackal and No Time to Die, while Essiedu will next be seen as Severus Snape in HBO’s Harry Potter reboot. Tovey, of Years and Years fame, also joined the group at The Savoy in London on Thursday to select the nominees, which will be announced in January. Related Stories Movies Sacha Gervasi's 'Darlington' Is a Tech Billionaire Film Unlike All the Others TV Gang Dong-won, Kim Go-eun to Lead Netflix's Period Romance-Action Drama 'The Twilight Between Us'

Presided over by Anna Higgs, managing director of production company Character 7, the panel also included director Molly Manning Walker (How to Have Sex), casting director Lucy Bevan (Barbie, F1, The Batman), producer Nira Park (Baby Driver, Shaun of the Dead) and We Are Parable creative director and BAFTA Film Committee deputy chair Anthony Andrews.

“Winning the EE Rising Star Award in 2022 was such a special moment in my career,” said Lynch, “so to now be on the other side of the table helping choose this year’s nominees feels like a real full-circle moment. I know first-hand how powerful it is to have people believe in your potential, and what excites me most is discovering performers who bring something completely their own to the screen. I’m incredibly proud to play a part in recognising this year’s rising stars.”

Essiedu added: “Every actor’s journey is different, and recognition at the right moment can be incredibly meaningful. What stood out during the judging process was the individuality and commitment each performer brought to their work. It was a privilege to help select five actors with such exciting potential, and I’m looking forward to seeing audiences champion them.”

Tovey, meanwhile, said the conversations around the table “showed just how much exciting talent is coming through.” He added: “I’m incredibly curious to learn who the public go for.”

#753. Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Every human body produces carbon dioxide simply by converting food into energy. Although the amount released by one person may seem small, the combined output of billions of people adds up to an enormous quantity.

A new study led by the University of Bath estimates that carbon dioxide production from human metabolism increased by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons annually. The researchers found that the dramatic rise was primarily the result of population growth, rather than a substantial increase in how much CO2 each person produces.

The findings could help scientists better understand the global carbon cycle, which describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and land. By measuring humanity's contribution more accurately, researchers hope to improve predictions about how well efforts to reduce carbon emissions will work.

Why Human CO2 Emissions Are Different From Fossil Fuels

Despite the enormous numbers, the researchers emphasize that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism is fundamentally different from the emissions generated by burning fossil fuels.

When people breathe out CO2, most of that carbon originally came from the food they consumed. Plants absorbed it from the atmosphere relatively recently, meaning it is already circulating through the natural carbon cycle.

Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is different. These fuels contain carbon that has remained trapped underground for millions of years. Burning them releases that long-stored carbon into the atmosphere, adding to the amount of CO2 circulating through the Earth's climate system.

The new research, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, was led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the University of Bath's Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism.

The team calculated that global CO2 production from human metabolism climbed from 1.18 billion metric tons in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons in 2015. More than 60% of that increase could be attributed to the growing number of people worldwide.

"We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven't had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

"What we've found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be."

How Scientists Measured Humanity's CO2 Production

To estimate how much carbon dioxide people generate, the researchers analyzed thousands of measurements collected from individuals across the human lifespan, from infants to older adults.

These measurements provided information about the CO2 produced by the body during ordinary daily activities. The team then combined those findings with worldwide population figures and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic CO2 production had changed over time.

The results showed that population growth was the dominant factor behind the 74% increase. Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide generated by individual people played a much smaller role.

Accurately measuring this process is important because human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment. Its influence on local carbon measurements can be especially noticeable in densely populated cities and urban areas, where large numbers of people live and work close together.

Understanding these contributions can help researchers develop more complete carbon budgets, which track the sources, movements, and destinations of carbon within the Earth's systems.

Scientists Stress That Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change

Although the study reveals a surprisingly large amount of CO2 production, its findings should not be interpreted as evidence that human breathing is a major cause of global warming.

The researchers are not recommending that people reduce their physical activity or change their diets to lower the carbon dioxide produced by their bodies. Instead, the goal is to make scientific measurements and calculations of the global carbon cycle more accurate.

Distinguishing between carbon dioxide produced through natural biological processes and carbon released by burning fossil fuels is essential for understanding the planet's changing climate.

Professor Gonzalez emphasized this distinction:

"The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We're not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

"What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs."

By establishing a clearer picture of humanity's metabolic CO2 production, the researchers have provided another piece of information scientists can use to track global carbon movements and evaluate strategies for reducing emissions.

At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS.

As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth? And if so, was it possible that this concerning signal was of Soviet origin — perhaps a spacecraft drifting helplessly into space, carrying a cosmonaut on board whose doomed mission had never been publicly acknowledged?

These strange events from November 1960 became the first in a series of alleged radio signal interceptions that would form the basis of an enduring Cold War-era mystery involving so-called "lost cosmonauts" — early Soviet space travelers rumored to have died during secret spaceflight missions before Yuri Gagarin's historic flight the following spring, in April 1961.Today, more than six decades later, the story remains one of the most haunting legends of the Space Age. Were there truly early Soviet space missions — with tragically ill-fated cosmonaut crews — that remain undisclosed to this day?

The peculiar story began in October 1957, as the Italian brothers Achille and Gian Battista Judica-Cordiglia learned, along with the rest of the world, about the Soviet Union's successful launch of Sputnik 1, Earth's first artificial satellite.

Immediately, the two became fascinated with the idea of trying to listen in on signals from such spacecraft and began working to assemble their very own radio tracking station, which they put together mostly from secondhand military surplus equipment. What they couldn't easily find and purchase, the brothers would often assemble themselves. They built an improvised tracking station in an abandoned World War Two bunker, which the brothers dubbed Torre Bert, that eventually became a fully functional radio facility with an antenna they built from salvaged materials like chicken wire and scraps of metal.

Whatever it lacked in aesthetics, the station made up for in functionality, and soon the brothers' amateur efforts reportedly allowed them to successfully intercept transmissions associated with Sputnik 2, the first Soviet spacecraft to carry a living creature into orbit: a dog named Laika, who became a one-way passenger on the mission. Later, the boys also said they were able to track transmissions from America's Explorer 1 satellite.

Some of what the Judica-Cordiglia brothers were able to achieve could be chalked up to being in the right place at the right time. Specifically, their location in northern Italy was advantageous, since it allowed them to monitor signals from Soviet spacecraft passing overhead.

By late November 1960, the Judica-Cordiglia brothers learned of reports from a West German observatory suggesting there may have been an unidentified satellite in orbit, raising an intriguing possibility: could there have been a spacecraft launch that had not been disclosed to the public?

Intrigued, the brothers began spending their evenings at Torre Bert scanning the skies for radio frequencies in search of the alleged mystery object. Eventually, they claimed to have detected a signal that differed significantly from those they had tracked in the past. Unlike the familiar electronic beeps they had intercepted from other satellites, this transmission seemed unmistakable: it was Morse code for SOS.

According to their account, as the pair listened to the alarming transmission, the signal gradually began to fade, raising a disconcerting possibility: what if the spacecraft they were monitoring hadn't merely been traveling through orbit, but had been drifting away from Earth?

If correct, the implications were staggering: the Soviet Union may have launched a secret space mission, but this time with a human cosmonaut on board — and something had gone terribly wrong, ending with a spacecraft and its occupant becoming lost in space.

Significantly, the brothers appear to have reached this conclusion independently, and no verified evidence has ever surfaced establishing that the transmission they claimed to have intercepted originated from a crewed spacecraft, let alone one associated with an unacknowledged Soviet mission that somehow escaped Earth's gravitational influence, with tragic results.

Nonetheless, the brothers' claims would soon help give rise to a disturbing possibility: that there had been unknown "lost" cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained hidden from public knowledge.

The alleged distress signal was only the beginning of a series of unsubstantiated claims the Judica-Cordiglia brothers made, and by the first days of February 1961, the amateur radio sleuths would claim to have intercepted another odd signal. This time, the pair claimed to have heard labored breathing coming across the airwaves, and even what resembled the strained moans of a person aboard an orbiting spacecraft.

In an equally eerie recording the brothers produced, what sounded like a rapidly beating human heart could be heard. The brothers shared the recording with Italian cardiologist Achille Dogliotti, whose examination reportedly led him to conclude that the sounds were consistent with strained breathing and an elevated human heartbeat.

With time, more recordings would begin to appear, featuring transmissions the boys believed to be evidence of unsuccessful Soviet missions that preceded the successful spaceflight of Yuri Gagarin, whose 108-minute journey around Earth in 1961 made him the first human to travel into space.

However, what may be the brothers' most controversial claim involved a recording they believed captured the final moments of a female cosmonaut whose ill-fated journey allegedly occurred prior to the historic 1963 spaceflight of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to travel into space. However, experts have pointed out that these transmissions do not follow typical military communications protocols, further casting doubt on their legitimacy.

As the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' notoriety increased, journalists and curiosity-seekers weren't the only ones whose attention they reportedly began to attract; their activities also allegedly garnered interest from intelligence officials.

In one instance, the brothers claimed a man identifying himself as a Russian reporter had visited them. Shortly thereafter, another individual — this time claiming to be an Italian counterintelligence agent — warned them that the "journalist" who had come to see them was a KGB agent.

The Judica-Cordiglias and their unconventional hobby, it seemed, had now placed them in the crosshairs of Soviet intelligence officials.

An unusual twist in this part of the Italian brothers' story would eventually emerge decades later, when London-based journalist Kris Hollington began reinvestigating their claims for a feature story that appeared in the paranormal-focused magazine Fortean Times. According to Hollington, a former Soviet KGB operative who later served as a Russian ambassador to a European country had reportedly confirmed (on condition of anonymity) that Moscow was indeed interested in the Judica-Cordiglias and their claims.

"Our cosmonauts were warned to be careful what they said while in space after this and we had the brothers followed," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington.

Things could have ended tragically for the brothers if it were not for the fame they achieved at the time for their alleged radio interceptions. As the former KGB agent told Hollington, it was believed for a time that the brothers "had to be dealt with — an accident perhaps," although after they appeared on a television program that brought them significant attention, any Soviet plans that would have endangered the brothers became impractical.

"That saved their lives," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington, who expressed gratitude for the circumstances that may well have saved the Italian brothers, with the former agent confiding to Hollington that he thought "they were good kids."

Of course, the claims of alleged Soviet surveillance are difficult to verify given the anonymity requested by Hollington's source. The same must be said of many of the claims made by the Judica-Cordiglias — even if the brothers were successful in intercepting Soviet transmissions at the time, that alone does not prove that they uncovered evidence of unacknowledged missions during which cosmonauts may have perished.

Some, like spaceflight researcher Sven Grahn, have acknowledged the genuine tracking capabilities the brothers possessed while remaining skeptical of the more sensational "lost cosmonaut" claims, suggesting the brothers might have misinterpreted some of the transmissions they recorded.

"I think that the Judica-Cordiglia brothers did run a tracking station and picked up signals from various spacecraft," Grahn said in an assessment of the brothers and their claims. "However, for some reason they thought that they needed sensational stories [to] maintain their image of a 'hot-shot' operation," he adds. "Once they over-interpreted some receptions and made fantastic claims they were 'trapped' and had to continue to produce sensations."

There is also the possibility that the recordings were hoaxes, of course. Whatever the case, there are no independently verified launch records, authenticated communications, or other evidence from the period that provides additional support for what the brothers claimed to have intercepted.

Something that can be verified, however, is the Soviet Union's well-documented secrecy, adding a further layer of complication to matters. As space historian James Oberg has observed, there are verified instances in which Soviet officials altered photographs and records from the early years of human spaceflight, a fact that has perhaps helped fuel rumors about alleged missing cosmonauts. It is also known that the Soviet space program covered up several deadly disasters, such as a launch pad explosion on Oct. 24, 1960 that killed a high-ranking Soviet military officer and at least 100 others. At the time, Soviet state news outlets reported it as a plane crash.

No verified evidence has emerged to support claims of failed, unacknowledged Soviet crewed spaceflights of the kind described in the lost-cosmonaut legends. Yet the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' accounts have drawn attention for decades and remain among the strangest stories in the lore of the early Space Age — a fact that illustrates humanity's enduring fascination with Cold War mysteries and phenomena that exist beyond Earth.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

#751. Thessaloniki Industry Awards: Georgian Road Movie ‘The Crossroad,’ North Macedonian Drama ‘They Bloom at Dawn’ Take Top Prizes

Georgian filmmaker Mari Gulbiani’s politically charged road movie “The Crossroad” and North Macedonian director Angela Dimeska’s female-centered drama “They Bloom at Dawn” took home the top honors at the Thessaloniki Film Festival’s industry awards Wednesday night.

Produced by Kate Kalandarishvili for Georgia’s Midifilm, Gulbiani’s fiction debut won the Two Thirty-Five Award, the top prize in the Agora’s Works in Progress section. The Crossroads Co-Production Forum, meanwhile, gave its top honors — the Frenel Post-Lab Post-Production Award — to Dimeska’s first feature, which is produced by Ognen Anton for North Macedonia’s Dream Factory. Related Stories Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese's 'What Happens at Night' With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE)

“The Crossroad” follows a young Muslim woman who, shortly after her wedding, learns that her husband has disappeared. Accompanied by her mother-in-law, she sets out on an emotionally charged journey to find him, only to discover that he’s travelled to Syria to join ISIS. The jury praised the film “for its ambition to craft a road movie across arid lands marked by hostility; for its documentary-inspired perspective on the resilience of those women left behind by men, war and religion; and for its embrace of imagination as their most powerful weapon.”

The top prize in the Crossroads Co-Production Forum went to “They Bloom at Dawn,” which follows a lost young woman seeking refuge in her grandparents’ lakeside village who must help her widowed grandmother save their threatened lake, forcing three generations of women to heal their fractured relationships and rediscover a sense of purpose.

“Life is full of surprises. It’s sad, it’s traumatic, but it’s also beautiful. Like the nature it portrays, these characters will also renew themselves and find ways to support each other, even when they can’t find the words for it,” the jury said in its citation. “This is a project that has a strong visual potential and a story that will resonate across borders. In fact, it’s a project that wants to break walls both in front of and behind the cameras, led by a director and a producer in sync, who moved us with their perfect pitch.”

The winner of the Onassis Film Award, which offers a cash prize of €10,000 ($11,100) to a Greek project participating in the Agora Works in Progress strand, went to the psychological thriller “Mignon,” by Sofia Georgovassili. Praising the “compelling, sharp story about the end of innocence,” the jury wrote: “A bold film with a suffocating atmosphere, exploring the limits of human endurance, the abuse that fuels closed social systems, the intensity of teenage friendship, the impulse to take risks and the inner strength of the powerless.” The film, which also won the €3,000 ($3,300) Agora Works in Progress Award from EKKOMED, is a ’90s-set story of moral decay told from the perspective of two teenage girls on a visit to the titular Athens department store.

Other Works in Progress winners included “The Law of the Flies,” a story of young love and new horizons from Turkish filmmaker Tunahan Kurt, which won the 119 Marvila Studios Award offering sound mixing services.

In the Crossroads Co-production Forum, Egyptian filmmaker Ayman El Amir won an €8,000 ($8,900) award for script development from France’s CNC for his dark comedy “A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon.” The ArteKino International Award, which offered a cash prize of €6,000 ($6,700), went to Turkish filmmaker Gözde Kural for “In Those Darkest Nights.” The Finos Film Award in the amount of €3,000 ($3,300) went to “Koukitsa,” from directing duo Christina Koutsospyrou and Aran Hughe. Lebanese actress and director Yumna Marwan also scooped a pair of prizes for her feature “This Is Not a Set.”

Here’s the complete list of winners of the Thessaloniki Film Festival’s Agora awards:

Two Thirty-Five Award: “The Crossroad,” Mari Gulbiani

119 Marvila Studios Award: “The Law of the Flies,” Tunahan Kurt

Agora Works in Progress Award by EKKOMED: “Mignon,” Sofia Georgovassili

ERT Agora Works in Progress Award: “Avanos,” Panagiotis Charamis

Neaniko Plano Subtitling Award: “Río Masacre,” Sylvie Weber

Onassis Film Award: “Mignon,” Sofia Georgovassili

Frenel Post-Lab Post-Production Award: “They Bloom at Dawn,” Angela Dimeska

CNC Award: “A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon,” Ayman El Amir

ArteKino International Award: “In Those Darkest Nights,” Gözde Kural

Finos Film Award: “Koukitsa,” Christina Koutsospyrou, Aran Hughes

Producers’ Network – Marché du Film Award: Sarra Ben Hassen, “A Touch of Paradise”

Midpoint Consulting Award: “The Arab of Your Dreams,” Patrick Tass

Greener Screen Consultancy Award: “This Is Not a Set,” Yumna Marwan

Sofia Meetings of the Sofia IFF Award: “This Is Not a Set,” Yumna Marwan

Mediterranean Film Institute Award: “In Those Darkest Nights,” Gözde Kural; “Fuoristagione,” Isabella Rinaldi

EAVE Thessaloniki Marketing Scholarship Award: Nada Riyadh, “A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon”

#750. Sam Levy, Jamie Ramsay Offer Advice to Up-and-Coming Cinematographers: “What You Guys Do Lives Forever”

At an in-depth conversation at the TorunCamerimage festival, the cinematographers behind 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York' and 'Being Heumann' discussed their inspirations, and the importance of trusting your gut. "Your greatest weapon as a DP is your intuition."

It would be hard to find two cameramen less alike than Sam Levy and Jamie Ramsay.

Levy, the Boston-born son of a classical violinist, who played for the Boston Symphony and the Boston Pops (and can be heard on a few soundtracks recorded by Boston Pops conductor John Williams, including The Empire Strikes Back) studied comparative literature and first considered a career as a diplomat before stumbling into film. He worked his way up, first as an assistant to acclaimed cinematographer Harris Savides (Zodiac, The Yards) before becoming, through collaborations with Noah Baumbach (Frances Ha, While We’re Young) and Greta Gerwig (Lady Bird), a defining visual voice in American indie cinema. Related Stories Movies Lashana Lynch, Paapa Essiedu, Russell Tovey Join Jury for BAFTA's Rising Star Award Nominees Movies Sacha Gervasi's 'Darlington' Is a Tech Billionaire Film Unlike All the Others

Ramsay, who grew up in South Africa, is a self-described “punk” who was kicked out of pretty much every school his parents sent him to, until he got accepted at the Academy of Film and Dramatic Art in Johannesburg. “That was the light turning on for me.”

His career trajectory has been distinctly international. Emerging from the South African film industry as a camera operator on Neill Blomkamp’s District 9 and through his longstanding partnership with director Oliver Hermanus (Beauty, Moffie), Ramsay has since established himself in British and international cinema through films like Andrew Haigh’s All of Us Strangers and Pressure from Australian director Anthony Maras.

Ramsay’s visual style tends towards a deliberately composed visual aesthetic — see his latest, Sian Heder’s 1970s historic drama Being Heumann — while a Levy-shot film, like his work on Noah Segan’s crime thriller The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, is more observational and fluid.

But the two found common cause at ToruńCamerimage, the Polish festival honoring the art of cinematography. Speaking to an audience of students and up-and-coming filmmakers, Levy and Ramsay eschewed technical talk about lenses, cameras and lighting techniques in favor of a more personal approach to filmmaking.

“It’s less about the how than about the why,” explained Levy. “Your greatest weapon as a DP is your intuition.”

In a wide-ranging conversation, the cinematographers discussed the formative moments in their careers, and the lessons they’ve learned along the way.

For Levy, his mentoring by Savides was key. “From the first day of working with Harris, I just wanted to be like him,” said Levy. “His knowledge was just so vast. He used to say: ‘Making a movie is very messy,'” said Levy, “it’s a moving train and it doesn’t stop.”

Levy recalled working as a camera loader on a commercial Savides was shooting, directed by Gus van Sant. The team was sent to “steal shots” in the subway in New York, working without filming permits. “Harris told me, ‘If anyone asks, tell them we’re doing a student film,'” Levy recalled. “We start and someone does come up. I tell them: ‘This is a student film.’ They say: ‘You’re shooting a student film with Gus van Sant?'”

Noting he was “never the tech guy,” Levy described how he finds an emotional way into the visual aesthetic of his films. The Only Living Pickpocket in New York stars John Turturro as Harry an aging wallet thief who finds himself out of sync with the modern world. It was shot on digital, on the ARRI Alexa 35, but to capture the analog nature of Harry’s profession, Levy decided to used Bausch & Lomb Super Baltar prime lenses, the same set famously used by Gordon Willis to shoot The Godfather.

Ramsay remembered the on-set confrontations and failures that he said led to his greatest breakthroughs as a cinematographer. “I’ve always been more driven by negatives than positives,” he noted. “If you say I can’t do something, then the rebel in me kicks in.”

But his only real confrontations he has had on set he said, “the only people I ever beef with” have been assistant directors “over time” and line producers “because of money. Because those are the two most important things you have as a cinematographer: Time and money.”

Levy and Ramsay described very different approaches to confrontations on set. Levy, “the would-be diplomat,” always tries to find common ground, he said. Ramsay, the rebel, “finds it hard to pander to something that doesn’t make sense to me.”

That two so different artists could achieve such acclaim, using such different methods, was the point of the Camerimage session. For both, the takeaway was the same: trust your instincts and the people you work with, and don’t let the craft get lost in the technique.

“What you guys do lives forever,” Ramsey told the young cinematographers in the room. “Think of that. It’s pretty immense. It’s pretty important. It’s worth doing everything you can to get it right.”

Japanese broadcasters will pitch nine TV dramas to buyers from across Latin America at MIP Cancun on Nov. 18, looking to secure remake deals, sales of the completed series and co-production partners in the region.

The Broadcast Program Export Association of Japan (BEAJ) is producing the 30-minute presentation, titled “Japan Session 2026: The Next Latam Hit Series from Japan.”

The session is one part of a larger “All Japan” presence at the market, which groups 10 Japanese broadcasters under the Japan Commercial Broadcasters Association (JBA). Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) is cooperating on the effort. Each of the nine broadcasters taking part chose one drama for Latin American buyers. Nicolás Smirnoff, an executive at Editorial Prensario and a FRAPA board member, will introduce the trailers in Spanish. The session is pitched around how each story could be adapted locally or co-produced, and buyers interested in a title will be steered to the rights holders at the Japan Pavilion, which the JBA is running, and through networking sessions.

Nippon Television Network Corp. is bringing “Punch-Drunk Woman,” while Tokyo Broadcasting System Television is presenting “Reboot” and Fuji Television Network has “kiDnap Game.” TV Asahi Corp. has selected “7 Secretaries” and TV Tokyo Corp. “Until I Destroyed My Husband’s Other Family.”

The remaining titles are Yomiuri Telecasting Corp.’s “Black Familia,” Tokai Television Broadcasting’s “Love and Hatred,” MBS’s “The Yakuza Boss’s Beloved” and Wowow’s “The Man of 0.5.”

“Latin America has a rich tradition of telenovelas, and we see significant potential for Japanese dramas with distinctive storytelling and original concepts,” said Sugiyama Makito, BEAJ’s executive director and the session’s executive producer. “By encouraging remakes and international co-productions, we hope to help Japanese content reach wider audiences in the region and create new business opportunities for the participating broadcasters.”

Smirnoff, who specializes in the Latin American audiovisual business, also represents Prensario International.

MIP Cancun is built around pre-booked meetings between buyers and sellers, with a focus on Latin America and Hispanic audiences in the U.S. For Japan’s broadcasters, the session is an attempt to bring stories first made for Japanese television into a region with deep telenovela roots.

The ice giants' skewed magnetic fields are a window into the high-pressure, high-temperature environment deep inside Uranus and Neptune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The posided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may stem from extreme conditions lying within their deep interior. Unravelling the mystery behind the magnetic fields of these worlds is giving us new insight into the little-known interiors of the ice giants.

Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune, the Voyager 2 spacecraft which spend past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. Voyager 2 found that their planetary magnetic fields were, to put it bluntly, wonky. Uranus’ magnetic field was offset from its rotational axis by 59 degrees and isn’t even centered on the planet’s core, but instead is only two-thirds of the way down. Neptune is similar, with a disordered magnetic field offset by 47 degrees and centered halfway between the core and its visible cloud tops.If we compare these planets to Earth, which has a stable magnetic field tilted by just 11 degrees to our planet’s rotation, we can see how extreme the magnetic fields of the ice giants are.

Various explanations for the strange magnetic fields of the ice giants have been put forward over the years. Uranus as a whole is tilted by 97 degrees and effectively rolls around the sun, and speculation is that billions of years ago it was knocked on its side by a collision with a long-lost Earth-sized planet. Could this collision have also skewed its magnetic field?

This might be a plausible explanation were Neptune’s magnetic field also not similarly skewed without having experienced a collision. Clearly, whatever the cause, it must be intrinsic to the nature of the two ice giant planets. Now, a new study by scientists in the U.S. and the UK, based on computer simulations and Voyager 2’s measurements of the two planets’ magnetic fields, may have found a solution.

The solution to the weird magnetic fields of the solar system's ice giants may come down to how planets generate their magnetic field through the dynamo effect. This arises from the swirling, convective motion of an electrically conducting liquid within a rotating body, which is able to generate and maintain a powerful magnetic field.

Inside Earth, the electrically conducting fluid is the molten iron in the outer part of our planet’s core, and the magnetic field that it generates has clear north and south poles – what we call a dipole, a phenomenon that we can also see in the two magnetic poles of a simple bar magnet.

However, the conditions inside Uranus and Neptune are somewhat different. As ice giants, they contain a lot of volatiles – ammonia, hydrogen, helium, methane, and water surrounding a probable rocky core. Furthermore, Uranus and Neptune are substantially larger than Earth, with 14.5 and 17 times the mass of our planet, respectively. This increased mass creates crushing conditions within the interior of the ice giants.

"Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," research team leader Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, who led the new findings, said in a statement. "Under those conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth."

Given the increasing electrical conductivity and the compositions of the two planets, the computer simulations were able to replicate the bizarre magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune. This showed how the magnetic-field structure co-evolves alongside changes in the fluid motion driven by convection and the temperature inside the planets.

It also seems that this co-evolution might not yet be over. The simulations indicate that the magnetic fields of both planets can change quite significantly in the space of just a few decades.

"Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," said Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches, the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others, it shifts only slightly over the same span."

NASA have prioritized a new mission to return to Uranus in the early 2040s, while the China National Space Administration’s Tianwen-4 mission launching to Jupiter in 2029 will deploy a small probe to carry onwards to Uranus via a gravitational slingshot. Until then, scientists are coming up with creative ways to not have to rely only on the 40-year-old Voyager 2 measurements of the magnetic fields.

For example, Tom Stallard of Northumbria University in the UK, who is a co-author with Yan on the new research paper, has been leading James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the faint infrared auroral lights on both Uranus and Neptune. Aurorae are generated when charged particles on the solar wind interact with a planet’s magnetic field, driving some of those charged particles into the atmosphere above the magnetic poles. (Neptune actually has a quadrupolar component, muddling its defined north and south magnetic poles.) As such, the location of aurorae is a good indicator of what’s going on with a planet’s magnetic field.

"We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere [upper atmosphere], promise to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, [which is] an important stepping stone," said Stallard.

The hope is that by combining JWST’s observations of the aurora with Voyager 2’s magnetic-field measurements and the results of the computer simulations, it will be possible to estimate the configuration of the magnetic fields on Uranus and Neptune today and see how they compare to the 1980s.

This would provide an experimental test to help show whether the new model describing the magnetic fields is on the right track, although we won’t know for sure until a new mission arrives in the ice giants’ backyard.

The findings were described on 3 November in the journal Communications Physics.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#747. Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot

Scientists have achieved a new world record by producing extraordinarily intense X-ray flashes that last just 300 attoseconds, an almost unimaginably brief period of time. Using the European XFEL, a powerful X-ray research facility, the team concentrated the flashes into an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair.

By squeezing so much X-ray energy into such a tiny space, the researchers created an exceptionally powerful beam that could open new possibilities for studying the behavior of electrons inside atoms and molecules. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists observe the rapid movements of electrons during chemical reactions and potentially even learn to control them.

The experiment took place in April 2026, and the findings have now been published in the scientific journal Optica.

Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes Last Just 300 Attoseconds

"This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse," says Ichiro Inoue from the University of Tokyo, first author of the publication.

Hard X-rays are a form of light with extremely short wavelengths. Scientists use two measurements to describe their extraordinary power. Fluence refers to the amount of energy delivered to a particular area, while intensity also considers how quickly that energy is delivered.

In this experiment, each X-ray pulse lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds (an attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second). Such incredibly short flashes offer researchers a way to investigate events that unfold far too quickly for conventional observation.

To concentrate the X-rays, the team used a specialized optical arrangement called an advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez, or AKB, system. It consists of two exceptionally precise mirrors that focus the beam in different directions. Each pulse underwent four reflections in total, with one mirror focusing the X-rays vertically and the other horizontally.

The result was an astonishingly small focal spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers (a nanometre is a billionth of a meter). By directing the energy into this microscopic area, the researchers were able to achieve record-breaking intensity.

"A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL," says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. "But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter."

These nonlinear interactions occur when extremely intense X-rays cause matter to respond in ways that would not normally happen under weaker illumination. Studying such effects could reveal new details about how atoms and electrons behave under extreme conditions.

An Extraordinary Reaction Inside Copper Atoms

To confirm the exceptional intensity of their X-ray pulses, the researchers directed them at a thin sheet of copper. The experiment provided independent evidence that the focused flashes reached peak intensities exceeding 10²⁰ watts per square centimeter.

When the X-rays struck the copper, they knocked electrons out of the atoms' innermost electron shells, leaving behind empty positions known as 'holes'. Electrons from other parts of the atoms then moved into these vacancies, releasing energy in the form of X-ray light.

Under ordinary circumstances, this emitted light travels in many different directions. However, when the incoming X-rays become sufficiently intense, something remarkable happens. The emitted light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to release additional X-rays traveling in the same direction, producing an amplified beam.

Scientists call this phenomenon amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

"It is almost magical to see this happening," says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument, where the study was conducted. "Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction."

The team also observed another important signature of extreme intensity. As they increased the energy of the X-ray pulses, the amplified signal initially became much stronger. At higher energies, however, the increase slowed and eventually leveled off, a behavior known as saturation.

This pattern is expected only under exceptionally intense X-ray illumination. Its appearance provided additional confirmation of the record intensity calculated from the pulse energy, duration, and size of the focused beam.

A New Way to Explore the Hidden World of Electrons

Beyond setting a world record, the breakthrough could significantly expand scientists' ability to investigate some of nature's fastest processes.

Electrons play a central role in determining how atoms bond together, how molecules interact, and how chemical reactions unfold. Their movements happen on extraordinarily short timescales, making them difficult to observe directly.

By combining ultrashort X-ray flashes with extremely high intensity, researchers hope to capture information about electrons before the incoming radiation has time to substantially alter the material being studied. This could provide a clearer picture of electron behavior inside atoms and molecules and, in the longer term, potentially lead to methods for influencing electron motion during chemical reactions.

The advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror system used for the record-setting experiment was transported from Japan. European XFEL is now preparing to receive its own AKB system, with delivery expected in early 2027.

The new equipment is being funded through a collaboration with the University of Hamburg, with additional support from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR).

Once the system has been installed and commissioned, scientists from around the world using the MID instrument are expected to gain access to these exceptionally brief and intense X-ray flashes. The upgraded capabilities could allow researchers to investigate electron behavior at a level of detail that has previously been difficult to achieve, bringing them closer to understanding and potentially controlling the fundamental processes behind chemical reactions.

#746. ‘Night Vision’ Is a DIY Film About a Mysterious Video Camera, Told in Dream Logic and With ‘Blair Witch Project’ Vibes

Christopher Yates discusses his first fiction feature, premiering at Tallinn, bending genres and minds, and exploring nightmares and trauma through a kaleidoscope to bring audiences "a big sack of fun."

Writer-director Christopher Yates knows the meaning of the phrase “indie filmmaking.” His fiction feature debut Night Vision (Öised nägemused) is a self-produced, low-budget film that bends genres and minds and immerses us in a story full of surprises, mystery and dream logic.

Co-written by Sandra Fassio, who also produced Night Vision with Yates, the film, which also features animated segments, gets its world premiere at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia. It debuts in its Rebels with a Cause Competition on Nov. 14. Related Stories Movies Rotterdam Film Festival, in Nod to 'Backrooms' and 'Obsession,' Sets Analog Horror 2.0 Focus Movies Sam Levy, Jamie Ramsay Offer Advice to Up-and-Coming Cinematographers: "What You Guys Do Lives Forever"

Night Vision follows Jenny, a young filmmaker in need of inspiration who can’t remember her dreams. Visiting a flea market with her crush Pierre, she buys an old video camera – only to find strange artifacts and “presences” on a tape in it. Can the camera maybe capture dreams?

“As Jenny is searching for a story to tell, the film unfolds as a shaky, moving parable that follows dream logic through free associations, tonal shifts, and genre-bending,” teases the PÖFF website, promising a blend of “autofiction, found footage, romance, and horror,” a “poignant diary film,” a “dreamcatcher that helps us relive the past” and “a rebellious act of filmmaking.”

The cast of Night Vision features Salomé Crickx, Pierre Gervais and Angelo Bison. The cinematographer was Leonor Malamatenios, with Matthieu Jamet-Louis handling editing.

Yates directed the 2009 documentary Not Here, a road movie about the rock band Girls in Hawaii, and co-directed Reveka (2015), a doc about the mines of Potosí in Bolivia. He is also the co-creator and co- writer of the Belgian series Public Enemy.

Now, he is ready to unveil his first fiction feature at Tallinn. Ahead of the world premiere, Yates talked to THR about his inspirations for Night Vision, shooting parts of it in his Brussels apartment, “the multitude of the departed” as a theme and those The Blair Witch Project vibes.

A lot of different ideas and influences have flown into Night Vision, with its exploration of dreams coming from the creator’s interest in our sleep experiences. “I’m a big dreamer and have been reading a lot, some a bit geeky stuff, about dreams,” Yates tells THR. “In addition to a lot of Freud, I have [amassed] a library of books over the years, even before I had a project about dreams.”

The core set-up for Night Vision suddenly popped into his minds, and it leant itself to an approach that fit his background in docs. “The idea of a camera filming dreams was literally something that came like this,” he recalls. “And I thought it could be good for a film with no money because it was about documentary-style filming.”Along with dreams, mourning and trauma also play a central role in Night Vision. “I lost my father when I was 20, not from suicide [which the film explores], but it was an experience of grief,” Yates explains. “And when you lose somebody, you often meet them in dreams, but in a casual way. You’re like, ‘But you’re supposed to be dead!’ You still have conversations with these people. And this is an inner experience that marks me.”

He also had a friend who died by suicide when he was 30, which he remembers as a traumatic experience. “Those experiences of dreams and grief combined with memory, and memory is like a kaleidoscope of things that I put together,” Yates tells THR. “There’s something about the multitude of people that disappear and do not have any trace of memory in the world. With everything going on nowadays in this world. with the wars, there’s something about the multitude of the departed that strikes me as something I’m working on in several ways. It’s not a theme in itself. It’s just a feeling.”

Fittingly, Graveyard of Memories is a potential film idea that Jenny mentions to Pierre after she buys the video camera. That scenes establishes an unusual dynamic between the two lead characters early on. “I had the idea of her being mean and reversing the classic roles between men and women,” Yates explains. “He’s a Labrador, as the actor says about his [character].”

The filmmaker, who has also worked as an editor, kept the creative process open, sharing that, “I love the process of creating while filming, letting yourself be surprised by reality,” as he has done in his documentary work. “I also wanted to give freedom to the actors, space so they could improvise, try stuff. The film was my lab for working with the actors, trying things, having fun. The two leads, Salomé and Pierre, were involved in the writing process. We improvised scenes I had written, and I’d rewrite things after their improvisation, and then they would re-improvise. The shooting happened in this huge friendship-like party zone. It was so much fun. There was just passion from the whole team.”

Yates shot part of Night Vision in his apartment in Brussels, where he and the creative team also worked on other parts of the movie. “For her voiceovers, Salomé repeatedly came back to my apartment because we needed some more,” the filmmaker recalls. “Actually, a lot of it was written during post-production.”

And working at home with his co-creators of Night Vision taught Yates a key lesson. “I love cooking,” he shares. “And I learned that cooking for your team, making pasta or mushroom sandwiches, really helps with having a happy team.”

Given the low-budget, self-made nature of the creative process, how did the Night Vision team create the film’s animation and special effects segments? “I watched a lot of YouTube tutorials to turn real footage shot on my iPhone into animation,” Yates tells THR. “I made some mistakes, but I did the animation and the special effects [, including for nightmare scenes,] myself. When the film had its first rough cut with bad animation and bad special effects, we went to ask for funding here in the French part of Belgium, and we got what’s called aide à la finition [post-production and finishing grants] to help finish the film. So, I managed to find professionals and pay them properly so they could do the animation and the special effects professionally.”

Not that the funding brought in a huge amount of money, with Yates describing it as “a little cash to properly pay” those animation and VFX experts. But in true DIY indie fashion, Yates highlights that everyone else worked on Night Vision out of passion for film. “Nobody was paid in this film,” he tells THR. “The whole crew worked on a participation basis, so it’s basically a percentage of whatever we might gross in the end, which will probably be zero, but who knows.”

As you can see in the Night Vision trailer above, parts of the film give off The Blair Witch Project vibes. “Obviously, that’s because it’s a found footage film, even if it’s in a documentary style,” Yates offers. “But I actually haven’t rewatched Blair Witch. I must have been about 20 or even younger when it came out. We were all blown away by it. It was a radical proposition. I have heard it still holds up today.”

What you may or may not notice immediately is how dream logic plays into the way Night Vision unfolds. “The basic narrative idea and structure of the film is the association of thoughts that you have in dreams,” Yates explains. “That’s why it jumps from one idea to the other seemingly randomly, and that’s why I created the idea of a film director who doesn’t know what she wants. So she jumps from one project to another and goes to memory.”

And you can find in Night Vision a meta cinephile discussion about film and its genres. “I am also making fun of the genres that you see a lot in Belgium, such as coming-of-age films,” says Yates. “I was trying to have fun with my knowledge of cinema and using all that to make it into a big sack of fun.”

What’s next for the creative? “Sandra, my girlfriend, my companion who is also the co-producer and co-writer of this film, and I are working on several projects,” Yates says. “I have a second feature in the writing [stage]. This new idea is about a nurse who gets hired into a rich house with a seven-year-old child in a coma from a swimming accident. But the nurse has a special telepathic skill and can hear what people feel inside. So, the film is an experiment in sounds. It’s still a bit in the horror genre, but once again with a twist.”

After all, Yates likes to push the envelope. “I love experiments,” he tells THR. “I love to think that if I throw three years of my life into creating a film, the audience should experience something that’s new, or at least something they haven’t seen before.”
